summary.text: A medically free 48-year-old man, referred from a family medicine clinic, presented to an ENT clinic with recurrent, mildly painful midline neck swelling for one and a half months, without dyspnea, dysphagia or signs of thyroid dysfunction and with no significant past medical, family, surgical or nutritional history. Examination was unremarkable apart from a small painless midline neck mass at the hyoid level, and flexible nasolaryngoscopy showed no noticeable lesion.

Ultrasound showed thin-walled fluctuant hypoechoic cystic structures; a TGDC was diagnosed, managed conservatively and followed with ENT and ultrasound every six months, and the Discussion says he was followed for an infected TGDC. After 1.6 years, ultrasound showed a 5 × 8 mm midline lesion and a 9 × 8 mm left thyroid nodule. FNA showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, Bethesda Level VI, and CT showed an infrahyoid cystic lesion suggestive of a TGDC.

He was offered hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy, chose total thyroidectomy, and underwent total thyroidectomy, the Sistrunk procedure and central neck dissection. Histopathology of the nodule gave classical papillary thyroid carcinoma (T1bN0aM0), 1.2 cm in the left lobe; the TGDC was free of papillary carcinoma and lymph nodes showed no metastasis.

Postoperatively he was doing fine with no complications and a clean surgical wound, and on day three he was discharged on 150 mg of levothyroxine. Follow-up clinical examination, ultrasound, CT and thyroid function tests were unremarkable, and the incision healed normally with no complications.
